subject: Neurology
subtopic: Effects of strokes by vascular territory
vignette: A 72-year-old man develops sudden weakness and numbness of the left leg. He has no facial or arm weakness and no aphasia or visual field defect. CT shows an infarct in the territory of the anterior cerebral artery.
question: Which of the following best describes the expected findings from an ACA infarct?

options.text: Contralateral paralysis and sensory loss of the lower limb with urinary incontinence
Contralateral paralysis and sensory loss of the face and upper limb with aphasia
Ipsilateral limb ataxia and intention tremor
Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
Ipsilateral facial paralysis and contralateral body pain/temperature loss

explanation_correct: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial motor and sensory cortices, where the lower limb is represented on the homunculus. An ACA infarct therefore produces contralateral paralysis and sensory loss of the lower limb. Urinary incontinence can accompany medial frontal (micturition center) involvement, while the face and arm are spared because they are supplied by the MCA.

explanation_incorrect.B: Contralateral face and upper limb weakness with aphasia is characteristic of an MCA infarct in the dominant hemisphere, not ACA.
explanation_incorrect.C: Ipsilateral limb ataxia and intention tremor localize to the cerebellar hemisphere, not the ACA territory.
explanation_incorrect.D: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing is characteristic of a PCA (occipital) infarct.
explanation_incorrect.E: Ipsilateral facial paralysis with contralateral body pain/temperature loss is a lateral pontine (AICA) syndrome, not ACA.

educationalObjective: ACA infarcts cause contralateral lower limb paralysis and sensory loss, often with urinary incontinence, because the leg is represented on the medial cortex.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Effects of strokes by vascular territory
vignette: A 64-year-old right-handed man develops sudden right facial and arm weakness, right-sided sensory loss, and difficulty speaking. He can understand commands but can barely produce words. CT shows a left MCA territory infarct.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's language deficit?

options.text: Infarction of the dominant (left) frontal lobe involving Broca area, with right face/arm weakness from MCA involvement
Infarction of the nondominant (right) parietal lobe causing hemispatial neglect
Occlusion of the anterior cerebral artery supplying the medial leg area
Infarction of the occipital lobe from posterior cerebral artery occlusion
Damage to the cerebellar vermis causing dysarthria

explanation_correct: The MCA supplies the lateral motor and sensory cortices (face and upper limb) and, in the dominant (usually left) hemisphere, the language areas: Broca area in the inferior frontal lobe (expressive aphasia) and Wernicke area in the superior temporal lobe (receptive aphasia). This patient's nonfluent speech with preserved comprehension and right face/arm weakness reflects dominant MCA involvement.

explanation_incorrect.B: Nondominant parietal lesions cause hemispatial neglect, not Broca aphasia; the lesion here is in the dominant hemisphere.
explanation_incorrect.C: ACA occlusion affects the medial leg area and would not cause aphasia or face/arm weakness.
explanation_incorrect.D: PCA occipital infarction causes visual field defects (contralateral hemianopia with macular sparing), not aphasia or face/arm weakness.
explanation_incorrect.E: Vermis lesions produce truncal ataxia and dysarthria, not aphasia or hemiparesis.

educationalObjective: Dominant MCA infarcts cause contralateral face/arm weakness plus aphasia (Broca or Wernicke depending on the site).

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Effects of strokes by vascular territory
vignette: A 59-year-old right-handed woman suffers a right MCA territory infarct and has left-sided weakness with neglect of the left side of her body and environment. A different patient with a left MCA infarct involving the temporal lobe has fluent but meaningless speech, impaired comprehension, and a right superior quadrant visual field defect.
question: Which of the following statements best accounts for these findings?

options.text: Wernicke aphasia is associated with a right inferior quadrantanopia from parietal lobe involvement
Hemispatial neglect is caused by dominant hemisphere lesions; Wernicke area lies in the nondominant hemisphere
Right MCA infarcts cause aphasia, whereas left MCA infarcts cause neglect
Both patients have lesions of the anterior cerebral artery
Nondominant MCA lesions cause hemispatial neglect; Wernicke aphasia from dominant temporal involvement is associated with a right superior quadrantanopia

explanation_correct: In the nondominant (usually right) hemisphere, MCA infarction produces hemineglect of the contralateral side. In the dominant hemisphere, Wernicke area in the superior temporal lobe is supplied by the MCA; Wernicke aphasia is associated with a right superior quadrantanopia because the temporal lesion involves optic radiation (Meyer loop) fibers carrying information from the contralateral lower retina.

explanation_incorrect.A: Wernicke aphasia is associated with a right superior (not inferior) quadrantanopia due to temporal lobe involvement.
explanation_incorrect.B: Hemispatial neglect is caused by nondominant (right) parietal lesions; Wernicke area lies in the dominant hemisphere.
explanation_incorrect.C: The pattern is reversed—dominant MCA lesions cause aphasia and nondominant lesions cause neglect.
explanation_incorrect.D: These are MCA territory findings, not ACA (which affects the leg).

educationalObjective: Nondominant MCA strokes cause hemineglect; dominant MCA Wernicke aphasia is associated with a right superior quadrantanopia.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Effects of strokes by vascular territory
vignette: A 60-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension develops sudden right-sided weakness. Examination shows right face, arm, and leg weakness with no aphasia, no neglect, and no visual field defect. CT shows a small infarct in the striatum and internal capsule.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Embolic MCA stroke from atrial fibrillation
Anterior cerebral artery infarct
Lacunar infarct of a lenticulostriate artery causing pure motor stroke
Posterior cerebral artery infarct with macular sparing
Basilar artery occlusion with locked-in syndrome

explanation_correct: The lenticulostriate arteries are small penetrating branches of the MCA that supply the striatum and internal capsule. Lipohyalinosis from long-standing hypertension causes lacunar infarcts in this territory, producing a pure motor stroke (contralateral face, arm, and leg weakness) without cortical signs such as aphasia, neglect, or visual field loss. It is the most common location of lacunar infarcts.

explanation_incorrect.A: A large embolic MCA stroke would involve the cortex and produce cortical signs such as aphasia or neglect, which are absent here.
explanation_incorrect.B: ACA infarcts cause predominantly leg weakness, not the face/arm/leg combination described.
explanation_incorrect.D: PCA infarcts produce visual field defects (hemianopia with macular sparing), not pure motor weakness.
explanation_incorrect.E: Basilar occlusion causes locked-in syndrome with quadriplegia and preserved consciousness, not a pure motor hemiparesis.

educationalObjective: Lenticulostriate lacunar infarcts from hypertensive lipohyalinosis cause pure motor stroke without cortical signs.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Effects of strokes by vascular territory
vignette: A 66-year-old man develops sudden visual loss. He has a right homonymous hemianopia with preservation of central (macular) vision. He can no longer read words although he can write normally. MRI shows an infarct in the left occipital lobe extending to the splenium of the corpus callosum.
question: Which of the following best explains this combination of findings?

options.text: Left MCA infarct involving Broca area with right homonymous hemianopia
Bilateral ACA infarcts involving the medial leg area
Right cerebellar hemisphere infarct with ipsilateral ataxia
Dominant (left) PCA infarct involving the occipital lobe and splenium, producing alexia without agraphia; the macula is spared because it has dual blood supply
Basilar artery infarct causing locked-in syndrome

explanation_correct: The PCA supplies the occipital lobe; occlusion produces contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing because the macula has dual blood supply from the MCA and PCA. When the dominant (left) PCA infarct extends to the splenium of the corpus callosum, it disconnects the visual cortex from the language area, causing alexia without agraphia. Nondominant (right) occipital involvement instead causes prosopagnosia, the inability to recognize familiar faces.

explanation_incorrect.A: Broca aphasia from a left MCA lesion causes nonfluent speech, not alexia without agraphia or hemianopia.
explanation_incorrect.B: ACA infarcts affect the leg and do not cause visual field defects or reading deficits.
explanation_incorrect.C: Cerebellar hemisphere lesions cause ipsilateral limb ataxia and intention tremor, not cortical visual or reading deficits.
explanation_incorrect.E: Basilar occlusion produces locked-in syndrome (quadriplegia, preserved consciousness), not isolated visual agnosia and alexia.

educationalObjective: PCA infarcts cause contralateral hemianopia with macular sparing; dominant+ splenial involvement causes alexia without agraphia and nondominant involvement causes prosopagnosia.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Effects of strokes by vascular territory
vignette: A 58-year-old man develops sudden double vision and right-sided weakness. Examination shows ptosis and a dilated left eye that is deviated —down and out— with loss of the left pupillary light reflex, along with right hemiplegia.
question: Which of the following best explains this syndrome?

options.text: Occlusion of the left anterior spinal artery causing medial medullary syndrome
Occlusion of paramedian branches of the PCA to the midbrain, causing ipsilateral CN III palsy and contralateral hemiplegia (Weber syndrome)
Occlusion of the left ACA causing leg weakness
A lesion of the right frontal eye field
Occlusion of the PICA causing Wallenberg syndrome

explanation_correct: Weber syndrome results from occlusion of paramedian branches of the PCA supplying the midbrain. It damages the ipsilateral oculomotor (CN III) fibers—producing ptosis, a dilated fixed pupil, and a —down and out— eye—and the adjacent cerebral peduncle containing corticospinal fibers, producing contralateral hemiplegia. Because CN III fibers traverse the midbrain, a midbrain lesion here gives an ipsilateral nerve palsy with contralateral hemiplegia.

explanation_incorrect.A: Anterior spinal artery occlusion causes medial medullary syndrome with contralateral paralysis/proprioception loss and ipsilateral tongue deviation, not CN III palsy.
explanation_incorrect.C: ACA occlusion affects the medial leg area and does not cause CN III palsy.
explanation_incorrect.D: A frontal eye field lesion causes conjugate gaze deviation, not a CN III nerve palsy with hemiplegia.
explanation_incorrect.E: PICA occlusion causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome with dysphagia, hoarseness, and Horner syndrome, not CN III palsy.

educationalObjective: Weber syndrome (paramedian PCA midbrain occlusion) causes ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral hemiplegia.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Effects of strokes by vascular territory
vignette: A 64-year-old woman suffers an acute basilar artery occlusion. She is fully alert and can blink and move her eyes vertically on command, but she cannot move her limbs, her face, or her tongue, and she cannot speak. She cannot move her eyes horizontally.
question: Which of the following best describes this patient's condition?

options.text: Persistent vegetative state from bilateral cortical destruction
Decerebrate posturing from a midbrain lesion
Locked-in syndrome from a ventral pontine lesion, with spared reticular activating system and vertical gaze centers
Wallenberg syndrome from PICA occlusion
Hemispatial neglect from a nondominant parietal lesion

explanation_correct: Basilar artery occlusion can infarct the ventral pons, damaging the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts (causing quadriplegia and loss of voluntary facial, mouth, and tongue movement) and the PPRF/CN VI nuclei (causing loss of horizontal eye movements). Because the reticular activating system is spared, consciousness is preserved, and because the midbrain vertical gaze centers are spared, blinking and vertical eye movements remain—this is locked-in syndrome.

explanation_incorrect.A: In a persistent vegetative state, consciousness and arousal are lost; this patient is alert with preserved vertical gaze, indicating an intact reticular activating system.
explanation_incorrect.B: Decerebrate posturing is extensor posturing from a lesion between the red and vestibular nuclei, not the preserved consciousness and vertical gaze described.
explanation_incorrect.D: Wallenberg (PICA) syndrome causes dysphagia, hoarseness, and Horner syndrome, not quadriplegia with preserved consciousness.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hemispatial neglect is a cortical (parietal) syndrome and does not cause quadriplegia or loss of horizontal gaze.

educationalObjective: Basilar artery occlusion can cause locked-in syndrome—quadriplegia and loss of horizontal gaze with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Effects of strokes by vascular territory
vignette: A 61-year-old man develops sudden vertigo, vomiting, and loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left side of his face and the right side of his body. He also has left-sided facial weakness, decreased tearing and salivation, decreased taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, left-sided hearing loss, and a left Horner syndrome.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: AICA (lateral pontine) syndrome, with involvement of the facial nerve nuclei and labyrinthine artery
PICA (lateral medullary) syndrome, with nucleus ambiguus involvement
Anterior spinal artery medial medullary syndrome
PCA occlusion with Weber syndrome
Isolated cerebellar vermis infarction

explanation_correct: AICA occlusion produces lateral pontine syndrome. Involvement of the facial nerve nucleus gives ipsilateral LMN facial weakness with decreased lacrimation, salivation, and taste over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue—findings specific to AICA lesions. The labyrinthine artery (a branch of AICA) supplies the inner ear, causing ipsilateral sensorineural deafness and vertigo; the spinal trigeminal nucleus and spinothalamic tract give ipsilateral face and contralateral body pain/temperature loss; sympathetic fibers give an ipsilateral Horner syndrome; and the cerebellar peduncles give ipsilateral ataxia.

explanation_incorrect.B: PICA (Wallenberg) syndrome affects the nucleus ambiguus, causing dysphagia and hoarseness—not the facial nerve, lacrimation, salivation, or taste findings described here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Medial medullary syndrome (ASA) causes contralateral paralysis/proprioception loss and ipsilateral tongue deviation, not crossed pain/temperature loss or facial nerve findings.
explanation_incorrect.D: Weber syndrome is a midbrain PCA lesion causing ipsilateral CN III palsy and contralateral hemiplegia, not these pontine/cerebellar findings.
explanation_incorrect.E: Isolated vermis infarction causes truncal ataxia, not the crossed sensory loss, facial weakness, and hearing loss described.

educationalObjective: AICA (lateral pontine) syndrome includes ipsilateral LMN facial weakness with reduced lacrimation/salivation/taste, hearing loss (labyrinthine artery), crossed pain/temperature loss, Horner, and ataxia.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Effects of strokes by vascular territory
vignette: A 55-year-old man develops sudden weakness of all four limbs along with loss of position and vibration sense in the limbs. His tongue deviates to the left when protruded. Sensation of pain and temperature is preserved.
question: Which of the following best explains these findings?

options.text: Right PICA occlusion causing lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome
Basilar artery occlusion causing locked-in syndrome
Occlusion of the PCA causing Weber syndrome
AICA occlusion causing lateral pontine syndrome
Occlusion of the anterior spinal artery causing medial medullary syndrome with ipsilateral hypoglossal dysfunction

explanation_correct: The anterior spinal artery supplies the medial medulla, containing the corticospinal tracts (contralateral paralysis), medial lemniscus (contralateral loss of proprioception/vibration), and hypoglossal fibers (ipsilateral tongue deviation). This is medial medullary syndrome (—Ants love M&M's—). Pain and temperature are spared because the spinothalamic tract runs laterally in the PICA territory. The tongue deviates toward the side of the hypoglossal lesion because the intact contralateral genioglossus pushes it toward the weak side.

explanation_incorrect.A: PICA (Wallenberg) syndrome affects lateral medullary structures, causing ipsilateral dysphagia/hoarseness, Horner, and crossed pain/temperature loss—not corticospinal or medial lemniscus signs.
explanation_incorrect.B: Locked-in syndrome from basilar occlusion features quadriplegia and preserved consciousness but not the ipsilateral tongue deviation or proprioception loss of a medullary lesion.
explanation_incorrect.C: Weber syndrome is a midbrain lesion causing ipsilateral CN III palsy and contralateral hemiplegia, not hypoglossal or proprioceptive findings.
explanation_incorrect.D: AICA (lateral pontine) syndrome includes facial nerve, vestibular, and crossed pain/temperature findings, not this medial medullary picture.

educationalObjective: ASA occlusion causes medial medullary syndrome—contralateral hemiparesis and proprioception loss with ipsilateral tongue deviation, sparing pain/temperature.
